claims_already_corrected_last_6_issues.claim: This is a unique opportunity for a true public-private partnership (DAF Alaska data-center land lease framed as a guaranteed-revenue PPP).
Uncrewed/autonomous systems in the High North enable persistence where continuous human presence is impractical.
Alaska is ~30 degrees cooler than Texas; PUE math saves a 1GW plant ~$150M/year (cooling/PUE advantage).
You might be looking at four or five cents a kilowatt hour for decades (cheap Alaska electricity for data centers, LNG-conditional).

orchestrator_dedupe_notes: AVOID re-litigating the energy-cost cluster (cheap power, PUE/cooling, DAF land-lease PPP) and Arctic uncrewed systems. Candidates tagged adjacency:'energy_cost_cluster' are close to recently corrected territory and should be weighted DOWN unless they attack a genuinely distinct mechanism. The two freshest, cleanest targets are the 'no AI policy / regulatory vacuum' claim and the 'fiber is the missing/gating ingredient' claim, both well-attributed and rebuttable from primary sources.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: Alaska has done none of that. No comprehensive policy, no clear direction, no coordinated strategy.
candidate_claims.claim_paraphrase_fair: Alaska lacks any comprehensive AI or data-center policy framework, leaving the state without direction or a coordinated strategy.

asserters.name: Roger Kaye
asserters.title_or_org: Freelance writer, Northern Alaska Environmental Center

candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: The 'no policy' claim is the justification for calls to create new legislative task forces, regulatory bodies, and public investment in AI governance infrastructure. If Alaska already has a meaningful policy substrate (statutes, a task force, executive directives, agency frameworks), the 'regulatory vacuum' narrative misstates the baseline and misdirects policy energy toward redundant structures rather than implementation.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: House Bill 47 criminalizing AI-generated CSAM passed the Alaska House unanimously Feb 27 2026; HCR 3 established a Joint Legislative Task Force on AI (introduced Jan 2026, advanced through committee); Alaska DEED released a K-12 AI strategic framework (Oct 2025); Alaska Bar Association issued Ethics Opinion 2025-1 on attorney AI use.
Governor Dunleavy ordered state agencies to use AI software as part of annual efficiency reviews in early 2026, an executive-branch AI directive even without a comprehensive AI law.
HCR 3 task force language and existence.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: ADN editorial board (Apr 2026); Kaye (Feb 2026); Rep. Gray ('Alaska is behind', Feb 2026); echoed in Fairbanks Daily News-Miner and Alaska Public Media. Most widely circulated meta-claim in 2026 Alaska AI press.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: the state's existing fiber system is too old, too small and too vulnerable
candidate_claims.claim_verbatim_alt: the missing ingredient to transforming that idea into reality is the need for fiber optic cable connections
candidate_claims.claim_paraphrase_fair: Alaska's current fiber infrastructure is the gating constraint blocking competitive AI data center development; without new trans-Arctic cable the state cannot compete.

asserters.name: Ethan Berkowitz
asserters.title_or_org: Co-founder, Far North Digital; former Anchorage mayor and state representative

asserters.name: Peter Asmus, Gwen Holdmann, Erlingur Gudleifsson
asserters.title_or_org: Researchers, Alaska Center for Energy and Power (ACEP), UAF
asserters.outlet: ACEP From the Grid blog, UAF

candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: The fiber-gap claim is the central reason investors and hyperscalers cite for not committing to Alaska data center projects, and it underpins Far North Digital's trans-Arctic cable capital raise plus the governor's 2029-2031 readiness timeline. If Alaska's fiber situation is materially better than claimed, investment timelines, subsidy logic, and public financing cases all shift.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: Quintillion's trans-Arctic submarine cable connects the North Slope to Southcentral and to the lower 48 via diverse routes since 2019; GCI and ACS reach Fairbanks and Anchorage with redundant paths. Dunleavy himself stated 'it's about 12 milliseconds from Alaska to the coast of Oregon' at Data Center World.
Alaska Communications announced a $124M NTIA BEAD-funded expansion (March 2026) delivering gigabit speeds to Anchorage, Fairbanks, Homer, Kenai, Kodiak, Soldotna and others in 2026.

The ACEP blog itself notes 'Alaska has had a fiber connection to the lower 48 since 2019' and that redundant high-capacity fiber currently extends to Fairbanks, Anchorage and the lower 48 via multiple diverse submarine routes, qualifying its own 'missing ingredient' framing.
prelim_counter_evidence.outlet: ACEP From the Grid blog, UAF

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Used by Berkowitz (Jan 2026), ACEP team (2024-2025), Gov. Dunleavy (Apr 2026), Schuerch (Mar 2026), Alaska Public Media (May 2026). Appears across pro-development and cautionary pieces. The verbatim 'too old, too small and too vulnerable' span is from the Berkowitz ADN op-ed; validator must confirm exact span on that page before use.

candidate_claims.claim_verbatim: They are highly capital intensive and employ many in the construction phase, but few for operation.
candidate_claims.claim_paraphrase_fair: AI data centers create substantial temporary construction jobs but very few permanent operational jobs for Alaskans.

asserters.name: Roger Kaye
asserters.title_or_org: Freelance writer, Issues Committee, Northern Alaska Environmental Center, Fairbanks

candidate_claims.why_load_bearing: How many permanent Alaskan jobs data-center development generates drives workforce investment by UAF and the state, and shapes the public-benefit case for tax incentives, land leases, and utility rate structures.

prelim_counter_evidence.fact: The proposed Stak Energy North Slope project is reported as a peak construction workforce of 1,500 with roughly 60 permanent jobs, partially confirming the 'few operational' claim for that project scale.
Loudoun County, Virginia derives 38% of total annual tax revenue from data centers, a fiscal-benefit counterframe even where direct headcount is modest.

candidate_claims.recurrence_note: Kaye in ADN (Jan 2026) and Fairbanks Daily News-Miner (Dec 2025); Rep. McCabe (Apr 2026); ADN letter (May 2026). NOTE: this claim is largely TRUE for operations headcount, so the corrective frame would be about fiscal/tax benefit and supply-chain effects, not a clean rebuttal. Weaker as a 'received wisdom is wrong' target.
